question: The arrow slits in medieval castle walls are only a few centimetres wide on the outside, but behind them the wall is cut away into a wide, funnel-shaped recess on the inside. Why were they built this way?
correct_answer: Wide firing angle, tiny target outside
alternative_answers: So the archer can aim in many directions while staying protected
Wider field of fire for the defender
Archer can shoot sideways and down but is hard to hit
Room to draw and angle the bow behind a narrow opening
Cover more ground without exposing the archer
headline_answer: Wide firing angle, tiny target outside
topic: Castles, palaces and famous houses
source_excerpt: The interior walls behind an arrow loop are often cut away at an oblique angle so that the archer has a wide field of view and field of fire.

extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Arrow slit article confirms the splayed interior gives a wide field of fire while the narrow exterior gives attackers a small target.

explanation: The inward splay, called an embrasure, gives the archer room to stand in the recess and swing the bow left, right and downward, so a single slit can cover a wide arc of ground below the wall. At the same time the outer opening stays extremely narrow, so enemy archers have almost nothing to aim at. The design maximises the defender's field of fire while minimising their exposure, and it also lets daylight into an otherwise dark wall passage.

question: In 1917 the British royal family dropped its German-sounding name and adopted a new surname taken from a castle. Which castle?
topic: Castles, palaces and famous houses
source_excerpt: Our House and Family shall be styled and known as the House and Family of Windsor

extra.why_interesting: Players know the royal family as 'the Windsors' and rarely stop to think the surname is barely a century old and was borrowed from a building.
extra.verification_notes: In 1917 George V adopted Windsor, named after Windsor Castle, replacing Saxe-Coburg and Gotha; the 1960 Mountbatten-Windsor addition doesn't change this.

explanation: George V made the switch during the First World War, when a German dynastic name had become a liability, and Windsor Castle remains the largest occupied castle in the world.

question: Graceland, the mansion where Elvis Presley lived and is buried, stands in which American city?
topic: Castles, palaces and famous houses
source_excerpt: 3764 Elvis Presley Boulevard (a segment of U.S. Route 51)

extra.why_interesting: Everyone knows the house; fewer can place it on a map, and Nashville is the tempting wrong answer.
extra.verification_notes: Graceland is in Memphis, Tennessee (Whitehaven neighborhood), and Elvis is buried there; no newer events change this (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graceland).

explanation: Elvis bought the house in 1957 and it sits in Memphis, Tennessee, not in Nashville as many assume.

question: Bran Castle in Transylvania draws hundreds of thousands of visitors a year as the supposed home of which fictional character?
topic: Castles, palaces and famous houses
source_excerpt: There is no evidence that Stoker knew anything about this castle

extra.why_interesting: The castle's entire fame rests on a fictional link that history does not support.
extra.verification_notes: Bran Castle is widely marketed as Dracula's Castle, linked to Count Dracula from Stoker's novel; the question's 'supposed' wording is accurate. I did not verify the visitor figure.

explanation: The link is pure marketing: Bram Stoker never saw the castle, and the real Vlad the Impaler likely never lived there either.

question: The 1919 treaty that ended the First World War was signed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles. In 1871, in that same hall, which empire had been proclaimed?
topic: Castles, palaces and famous houses
source_excerpt: The German Empire was proclaimed on January 18, 1871, in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles

extra.why_interesting: Players know the 1919 treaty but not that France chose the room precisely because Germany had humiliated it there half a century earlier.
extra.verification_notes: The German Empire was proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles on 18 January 1871, as the Wikipedia article states.

explanation: Wilhelm I was declared German Emperor there after defeating France, which is exactly why the French insisted on the same room for Germany's surrender terms in 1919.

question: The Alhambra palace in Granada takes its name from an Arabic word meaning 'the one of which colour'?
topic: Castles, palaces and famous houses
source_excerpt: al-Ḥamrāʼ, meaning 'the red one' (full form al-Qalʻah al-Ḥamrāʼ, 'the red fortress')

extra.why_interesting: Players picture the Alhambra's white interiors and cool fountains, so the colour hidden in its name surprises them.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Alhambra's name derives from Arabic al-Ḥamrāʼ, 'the red one'; no newer development affects this.

explanation: Al-Hamra means 'the red one', after the reddish tone of its outer walls, especially at sunset.

question: In 1618 two imperial governors were thrown out of a window of Prague Castle. The incident is regarded as the start of which European war?
topic: Castles, palaces and famous houses
source_excerpt: This act precipitated the Bohemian Estates' Revolt and ultimately sparked the Thirty Years' War.

extra.why_interesting: A fit of window-throwing in one castle set off three decades of war across Europe, and the victims survived the fall.
extra.verification_notes: The 1618 Defenestration of Prague is widely regarded as the start of the Thirty Years' War (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defenestrations_of_Prague).

explanation: All three men survived the roughly twenty-metre fall, reportedly landing in a dung heap, but the Thirty Years' War that followed devastated central Europe.

question: The grounds of which Viennese palace contain the world's oldest zoo still in operation, founded in 1752?
topic: Castles, palaces and famous houses
source_excerpt: the world's oldest zoo still in operation

extra.why_interesting: Players associate the Habsburgs with palaces and portraits, not with running a menagerie that outlived the dynasty itself.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Tiergarten Schönbrunn, in the grounds of Schönbrunn Palace, was established in 1752 and is the world's oldest zoo still in operation.

explanation: The Habsburg menagerie at Schönbrunn opened in 1752 and is still running today, long after the imperial family that built it lost its throne.

question: Newspaper tycoon William Randolph Hearst's hilltop estate in California inspired Xanadu, the vast mansion in which 1941 film?
topic: Castles, palaces and famous houses
source_excerpt: Hearst Castle in San Simeon, California, has been considered to be the main inspiration for Xanadu

extra.why_interesting: The film's grotesque fictional mansion was modelled on a real house, and the real owner was so stung he tried to bury the film.
extra.verification_notes: Xanadu is Kane's mansion in Citizen Kane (1941), and Hearst Castle is considered its main inspiration, per Wikipedia.

explanation: Orson Welles modelled Charles Foster Kane's Xanadu on Hearst Castle, and Hearst used his newspapers to try to suppress the film.

question: True or false: Edinburgh Castle is built on top of an extinct volcano.
topic: Castles, palaces and famous houses
source_excerpt: The castle stands upon the plug of an extinct volcano, which is estimated to have risen about 350 million years ago during the lower Carboniferous period.

extra.why_interesting: A volcano under a Scottish castle sounds like a tourist tall tale, yet it is plain geology.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia states Edinburgh Castle stands on the plug of an extinct volcano from about 350 million years ago, so True is correct.

explanation: Castle Rock is a volcanic plug roughly 350 million years old, which is why the castle has such steep cliffs on three sides.

question: The Forbidden City in Beijing was completed as the imperial palace in which year?
topic: Castles, palaces and famous houses
source_excerpt: The Forbidden City was constructed from 1406 to 1420, and was the imperial palace and winter residence of the Emperor of China from the Ming dynasty.

extra.why_interesting: Players tend to guess the palace is either ancient or far more recent; placing it alongside the European late Middle Ages is the surprise.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia states the Forbidden City was constructed 1406 to 1420, matching the answer 1420 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbidden_City).

explanation: Construction ran from 1406 to 1420 under the Ming Yongle Emperor, so the palace was finished decades before Columbus sailed.

question: Malbork Castle in northern Poland is the largest castle in the world by land area. Which order of crusading knights built it as their headquarters?
topic: Castles, palaces and famous houses
source_excerpt: It is the largest castle in the world measured by land area.

extra.why_interesting: Players expect the world's biggest castle to be a royal seat, not the headquarters of a crusading order of monks.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Teutonic Order built Malbork and that it is the largest castle in the world by land area; no newer development contradicts this.

explanation: The Teutonic Order began the brick fortress in the 1270s and ran its Baltic state from there, which explains why a castle this big belongs to monks rather than a king.

question: Himeji, Japan's best-preserved feudal castle, is nicknamed after which white bird, thanks to its bright plastered walls and wing-like roofs?
topic: Castles, palaces and famous houses
source_excerpt: Hakuro-jō or Shirasagi-jō (White Heron Castle) because of its brilliant white exterior and supposed resemblance to a bird taking flight.

extra.why_interesting: Players can picture the white walls but must reason toward the right bird, with swans and cranes as tempting near-misses.
extra.verification_notes: Himeji Castle is widely known as White Heron Castle (Shirasagi-jō) because of its white exterior and its resemblance to a bird in flight; nothing newer contradicts this.

explanation: It is known as the White Heron Castle, and its hilltop walls and layered roofs are meant to resemble a heron taking flight.

question: At the Château de Chambord in France's Loire Valley, two people can climb the grand central staircase at the same time, keep catching sight of each other on the way up, and yet never cross paths. What shape is this famous staircase?
topic: Castles, palaces and famous houses
source_excerpt: The two spirals ascend the three floors without ever meeting, illuminated from above by a sort of light house at the highest point of the château.

extra.why_interesting: The player assumes a staircase is a staircase; the puzzle of 'always in view, never meeting' sounds like a magic trick until the double-spiral shape clicks and it feels obvious in hindsight.
extra.verification_notes: Chambord's central staircase is a double-spiral (double-helix) design where two ascents never meet, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Château_de_Chambord

explanation: Two separate spiral flights twist around one open central core, so each climber glimpses the other through the openings but stays on their own ramp. The design is widely linked to Leonardo da Vinci, who died at nearby Amboise in 1519, the very year construction began.

question: An 1878 quarrel over who owned a hog helped ignite America's most notorious family feud, fought along the Kentucky–West Virginia border. Name the two families.
topic: Famous rivalries, duels and feuds in history
source_excerpt: Floyd Hatfield, a cousin of Devil Anse, owned the hog, but Randall McCoy claimed it was his, saying that the notches on the pig's ears were McCoy

extra.why_interesting: Players know the names as shorthand for any family feud but rarely know it escalated from a quarrel over a single pig.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the 1878 hog dispute between Floyd Hatfield and Randall McCoy on the WV–KY border; no newer developments affect it.

explanation: The feud ran for more than a decade and killed around a dozen people, which makes a disputed pig a very expensive animal.

question: According to the famous story, Ferruccio Lamborghini started building sports cars after Enzo Ferrari dismissed his complaint about a Ferrari's clutch. What vehicles had made Lamborghini rich in the first place?
topic: Famous rivalries, duels and feuds in history
source_excerpt: the story is as much the stuff of legend as it is of fact.

extra.why_interesting: The glamour brand was born from a farm-machinery magnate's wounded pride; the humble answer is the delight.
extra.verification_notes: Lamborghini's wealth came from tractors (Lamborghini Trattori, founded 1948), and the question is framed as 'the famous story', so the legend's uncertain status doesn't matter.

explanation: Lamborghini Trattori is still in business today, so the raging bull on the badge has farm roots as well as racing ones.

question: Which Asian city hosted the brutal third fight between Muhammad Ali and Joe Frazier in 1975, lending the bout its famous rhyming nickname?
topic: Famous rivalries, duels and feuds in history
source_excerpt: The contest's name is derived from Ali's rhyming boast that the fight would be 'a killa and a thrilla and a chilla, when I get that gorilla in Manila.'

extra.why_interesting: The rhyming-nickname clue gives a path even to players who only half-remember the bout.
extra.verification_notes: Third Ali-Frazier fight on Oct 1, 1975 is the 'Thrilla in Manila' (venue technically in Quezon City, Metro Manila), so 'Manila' fits the nickname-based question; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrilla_in_Manila

explanation: Ali won when Frazier's corner stopped the fight before the final round, and he later said it was the closest he had ever come to dying.

question: The 1972 'Match of the Century', in which American Bobby Fischer took the world chess title from Soviet champion Boris Spassky, was played in which capital city?
topic: Famous rivalries, duels and feuds in history
source_excerpt: The match took place in the Laugardalshöll in Reykjavík, Iceland

extra.why_interesting: A Cold War showdown between an American and a Soviet took place in a tiny neutral capital most players can picture once they think of it.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the 1972 Fischer–Spassky match was held in Reykjavík, Iceland's capital, and Fischer won 12½–8½.

explanation: Fischer nearly didn't turn up and forfeited the second game, yet he still became the first American world champion.

question: True or false: when Andrew Jackson became US president in 1829, he still had a bullet from a duel lodged in his chest.
topic: Famous rivalries, duels and feuds in history
source_excerpt: this particular bullet was never removed

extra.why_interesting: It sounds like exaggerated frontier legend, which is exactly why the true answer lands.
extra.verification_notes: Dickinson's 1806 bullet stayed lodged in Jackson's chest for life (the bullet removed in 1832 was the separate Benton one), so it was still there in 1829; source is a secondary health history, not a primary document.

explanation: Jackson took the shot near his heart in an 1806 duel, then calmly raised his pistol and killed his opponent, Charles Dickinson. Surgeons judged the bullet too dangerous to remove.

question: Three of these men died from wounds suffered in a duel. Which one fought a duel and lived to tell the tale?
topic: Famous rivalries, duels and feuds in history
source_excerpt: Wellington fired first and missed... Winchilsea deliberately fired into the air, then apologized for his inflammatory letter.

extra.why_interesting: The surprise is double: Wellington is the only survivor, and he fought his duel as sitting head of government.
extra.verification_notes: Wellington fought Winchilsea in 1829 and both survived; Hamilton, Pushkin and Galois all died of duel wounds.

explanation: Wellington fought the Earl of Winchilsea in 1829 while serving as British Prime Minister; both men deliberately missed. Hamilton, Pushkin and Galois were all killed.

question: Isaac Newton accused a German philosopher of stealing calculus, and the Royal Society's report backing Newton was, in reality, drafted by Newton himself. Who was the rival?
topic: Famous rivalries, duels and feuds in history
source_excerpt: The report of the committee, finding in favor of Newton, was written and published early in 1713 as the 'Commercium Epistolicum' (mentioned above) by Newton himself.

extra.why_interesting: The stem's 'secretly wrote the verdict' detail is the hook; the answer is winnable for anyone who knows calculus has two fathers.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Newton himself wrote the Royal Society's report favouring him in the calculus dispute with Leibniz.

explanation: Historians now agree both men invented calculus independently, and it is Leibniz's notation, not Newton's, that students use today.

question: During the 1880s 'War of the Currents', Thomas Edison quietly backed building the first electric chair with his rival's alternating current, hoping to brand it as deadly. Which industrialist was the rival?
topic: Famous rivalries, duels and feuds in history
source_excerpt: it would be best to use current generated by 'alternating machines,' manufactured principally in this country by Geo. Westinghouse.

extra.why_interesting: The player expects Tesla, but the industrialist Edison actually targeted was Westinghouse, and the verb suggestion is pure spite.
extra.verification_notes: Edison and Harold Brown promoted Westinghouse AC for the electric chair, and Westinghouse generators were covertly acquired for it (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_currents).

explanation: Edison even proposed that executed criminals be described as having been 'Westinghoused'. The name never caught on, but Westinghouse's AC won the war anyway.

question: In 1859 the United States and Britain nearly went to war over San Juan Island, off the Pacific coast of North America. The standoff is named after its only casualty. What animal was it?
topic: Famous rivalries, duels and feuds in history
source_excerpt: Despite being referred to as a 'war', there were no human casualties on either side, only a pig.

extra.why_interesting: Two empires nearly went to war and the only death was a farm animal; players can reason toward a creature a farmer would shoot.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Pig War's only casualty was a pig shot by Lyman Cutlar; no contradicting sources or later developments found.

explanation: An American farmer shot a British company's pig for raiding his potato patch, warships gathered, and the island was eventually awarded to the US by the German Kaiser as arbitrator.

question: Feuding brothers Adi and Rudolf Dassler split their family shoe business and founded two rival brands in the same small Bavarian town. Which brand was registered first?
topic: Famous rivalries, duels and feuds in history
source_excerpt: Adolf formed a company registered as Adidas AG, from Adi Dassler, on 18 August 1949

extra.why_interesting: Adidas is the bigger, more famous brand, so most players assume it came first; the smaller rival actually did.
extra.verification_notes: Puma/RUDA was registered in 1948 (Puma name Oct 1948), before Adidas AG on 18 Aug 1949, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adidas.

explanation: Rudolf set up Puma in 1948 and Adi registered Adidas the following year. Their hometown of Herzogenaurach became known as the town of bent necks, because people checked your shoes before deciding whether to talk to you.

question: Which French mathematician spent the night before his fatal 1832 duel frantically writing up his theory of equations, then died the next day aged just 20?
topic: Famous rivalries, duels and feuds in history
source_excerpt: stayed up all night writing letters to his Republican friends and composing what would become his mathematical testament, the famous letter to Auguste Chevalier

extra.why_interesting: The tragic image of a 20-year-old racing to save his mathematics before dawn is the hook; the name is reachable for anyone who has met Galois theory.
extra.verification_notes: Galois died 31 May 1832 aged 20 after a duel and wrote his mathematical testament the night before; the 'frantic' detail is a popular legend but the answer is unambiguous.

explanation: His notes, scrawled with pleas of 'I have no time', founded what is now called Galois theory and finally explained why some equations cannot be solved by formula.

question: The vicious 19th-century feud between rival American fossil hunters Othniel Marsh and Edward Cope, which gave us Stegosaurus and Triceratops, is remembered by what warlike two-word name?
topic: Famous rivalries, duels and feuds in history
source_excerpt: a period of intense and ruthlessly competitive fossil hunting

extra.why_interesting: A scientific feud so vicious it involved bribery and dynamiting fossil sites, and it gave the world its best-loved dinosaurs.
extra.verification_notes: The Marsh–Cope feud is universally called the Bone Wars; Stegosaurus and Triceratops were both Marsh's names, and no newer development affects it (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bone_Wars).

explanation: The pair bribed workers, spied on each other and reportedly destroyed dig sites rather than let the other have them, yet between them they named well over a hundred new species.

question: In August 1995 the 'Battle of Britpop' saw Blur and Oasis release singles on the same day. Oasis offered 'Roll With It'. Which Blur song beat it to number one?
topic: Famous rivalries, duels and feuds in history
source_excerpt: Blur's 'Country House' sold 274,000 copies, charting at number one in the best week for UK singles sales in a decade

extra.why_interesting: The chart battle is famous, but recalling which Blur single actually won is the real test.
extra.verification_notes: Country House by Blur beat Oasis's Roll With It to number one in the August 1995 chart battle, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Britpop.

explanation: Blur won the battle but Oasis arguably won the war, since their album 'What's the Story Morning Glory' went on to sell many times more than Blur's 'The Great Escape'.

question: In 1948, two brothers in the small German town of Herzogenaurach split their family shoe company and reportedly never spoke again. Each went on to found a global sportswear brand. Name both brands.
topic: Famous rivalries, duels and feuds in history
source_excerpt: Once the brothers divided their businesses they never spoke again.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume two global rivals must come from different corners of the world; in fact they were born in a feud between two brothers in one small Bavarian town, where the two factories still face each other across the river.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the 1948 split of Adolf and Rudolf Dassler into Adidas and Puma, and that they never spoke again.

explanation: Adolf 'Adi' Dassler built Adidas from his own nickname and surname, while his brother Rudolf founded Puma across the river. The feud divided the whole town, which was nicknamed the town of bent necks because locals checked strangers' shoes before deciding whether to talk to them.

question: In 1804, Alexander Hamilton was shot dead in a duel by a man who at that moment held which office in the United States government?
correct_answer: Vice President of the United States
topic: Famous rivalries, duels and feuds in history
source_excerpt: Burr returned fire and hit Hamilton in the lower abdomen above the right hip.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture duels as the business of hot-headed officers and gentlemen on the fringe of public life. The payoff is that Hamilton's killer was no fringe figure but the second-highest official in the US government, who then simply went back to presiding over the Senate.
extra.verification_notes: Aaron Burr, sitting Vice President, fatally shot Hamilton in the July 11, 1804 duel; Hamilton died the next day, which is a minor wording imprecision in 'shot dead'.

explanation: Aaron Burr was serving as Thomas Jefferson's Vice President when he fatally shot Hamilton at Weehawken, New Jersey, and he finished his term in office despite murder charges in two states.

question: Strip away its thin outer plating, and an Olympic gold medal is made almost entirely of which metal?
topic: Gold and precious metals
source_excerpt: It is composed at least 92.5% of silver, plated with 6 grams of gold.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a gold medal is gold through and through; it is actually a silver medal wearing a thin gold coat.
extra.verification_notes: Olympic gold medals must be at least 92.5% silver plated with 6 g of gold per IOC rules; no change found for 2026 or 2028.

explanation: Olympic rules only require about six grams of gold as plating, so the medal underneath is sterling-grade silver, over 92 percent pure.

question: If every gram of gold ever mined in human history were melted into one solid cube, roughly how long would each side be?
topic: Gold and precious metals
source_excerpt: If all this gold were collected into a single cube, it would measure just 22 metres on each side.

extra.why_interesting: Centuries of gold rushes, bank vaults and treasure fleets feel like mountains of metal, yet the whole lot would fit comfortably inside a tennis court footprint.
extra.verification_notes: WGC says about 222,600 tonnes of gold have been mined, which forms a cube about 22 m per side, so 'About 20 metres' is the closest option (https://www.gold.org/goldhub/data/how-much-gold).

explanation: All the gold humanity has ever dug up is only around 200,000 tonnes, and gold is so dense that this fits in a cube about 22 metres on a side, shorter than a seven-storey building.

question: The carat, the unit jewellers use to weigh gemstones, takes its name from the seed of which tree?
topic: Gems
source_excerpt: comes from Italian carato, which comes from Arabic (qīrāṭ; قيراط), in turn borrowed from Greek kerátion κεράτιον 'carob seed'

extra.why_interesting: The carat sounds like a precise, laboratory-born unit; it is actually named after a bean that merchants trusted to be reasonably uniform in weight.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's etymology for carat traces it via Italian carato and Arabic qirat to Greek kerátion, 'carob seed', so the claimed answer is correct.

explanation: Ancient traders used the small, fairly uniform seeds of the carob tree as counterweights for gems, and today's carat is fixed at exactly one fifth of a gram.

question: Ruby and sapphire are simply different colours of the same mineral, second only to diamond in hardness. Which mineral?
topic: Gems
source_excerpt: Corundum has two primary gem varieties: ruby and sapphire.

extra.why_interesting: Ruby and sapphire are sold and priced as separate gems, yet they are chemically the same stone with different impurities.
extra.verification_notes: Ruby and sapphire are both gem varieties of corundum, Mohs 9 and second only to diamond on the Mohs scale; the moissanite hardness caveat doesn't change the answer (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corundum).

explanation: Corundum is aluminium oxide; a trace of chromium turns it ruby red, while iron and titanium give sapphire blue, and it scores nine on the Mohs hardness scale.

question: The golden gemstone amber, famous for sometimes trapping ancient insects inside it, started out as what?
topic: Gems
source_excerpt: Amber is fossilized tree resin.

extra.why_interesting: A warm, glassy gem that occasionally traps whole insects is not a mineral at all but the hardened sap of ancient forests.
extra.verification_notes: Amber is fossilized tree resin per Wikipedia; no ambiguity or newer developments found.

explanation: Amber is sticky resin that oozed from trees tens of millions of years ago and slowly hardened into a gem, which is why insects and even small lizards can be found sealed inside.

question: Which blue-violet gemstone, first discovered in 1967, is mined commercially in only one small area of hills near Mount Kilimanjaro?
topic: Gems
source_excerpt: Tanzanite is only found in Simanjiro District of Manyara Region in Tanzania, in a very small mining area approximately 7 km long and 2 km wide near the Mererani Hills.

extra.why_interesting: A gem that is a thousand times rarer than diamond by location exists in a single patch of hills; the Kilimanjaro clue lets a player reason their way to the name.
extra.verification_notes: Tanzanite was discovered in 1967 and is found only in a tiny area of the Mererani hills in Tanzania, per Wikipedia.

explanation: Tanzanite comes solely from the Merelani Hills in northern Tanzania, and Tiffany and Company gave the stone its name after the country when it launched it to the world in 1968.

question: Around 95 percent of the world's precious opal comes from a single country, where miners in one outback town live in underground homes to escape the heat. Which country?
topic: Gems
source_excerpt: Australian opal has been cited as accounting for 95–97% of the world's supply of precious opal

extra.why_interesting: Players tend to associate gem mining with Africa, India or South America; one country's desert towns supply almost all of a single famous gem.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia states Australia accounts for 95–97% of the world's precious opal, and Coober Pedy residents live in underground homes; I found no newer development that contradicts this.

explanation: Opal is Australia's national gemstone, and in the mining town of Coober Pedy many residents live in cool dugouts carved into the rock.

question: True or false: of all the metals, gold is the best conductor of electricity.
topic: Gold and precious metals
source_excerpt: Silver 63.0×10⁶ S/m; Copper 59.6×10⁶ S/m; Gold 41.1×10⁶ S/m (conductivity at 20°C; paraphrased from the article's table)

extra.why_interesting: Gold-plated audio cables and connectors make people assume gold conducts best; it is used for its resistance to tarnish, while humbler silver actually wins on conductivity.
extra.verification_notes: Silver (63.0×10⁶ S/m) and copper (59.6×10⁶ S/m) both conduct better than gold (41.1×10⁶ S/m), so the statement is false, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_resistivity_and_conductivity

explanation: Silver is the best electrical conductor of any metal, with copper second and gold only third; gold earns its place on connectors because it never tarnishes.

question: The Black Prince's Ruby, the huge red stone on the front of the British Imperial State Crown, is not a ruby at all. Which red gemstone is it really?
topic: Jewellery
source_excerpt: It was not until 1783 that spinels were chemically differentiated from rubies.

extra.why_interesting: One of the most famous 'rubies' in the world, worn by English kings for six centuries, turned out to be a different mineral entirely once gemmology could tell them apart.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Black Prince's Ruby is a 170-carat red spinel set in the Imperial State Crown, with no recent changes noted.

explanation: For centuries nobody could distinguish red spinel from ruby, so several famous royal 'rubies' turned out to be spinel, including this 170-carat stone said to have been worn by Henry the Fifth at Agincourt.

question: Platinum's name comes from a Spanish word meaning a 'little' or lesser version of which other precious metal?
topic: Gold and precious metals
source_excerpt: Its name originates from Spanish platina, a diminutive of plata 'silver'.

extra.why_interesting: Today platinum is the aristocrat of jewellery metals, yet its name is a dismissive nickname given by people who threw it away as a cheap impostor of another metal.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Platinum article confirms the name derives from Spanish platina, a diminutive of plata 'silver'.

explanation: Spanish colonists in South America called the grey nuggets 'platina', little silver, and considered them a nuisance that contaminated their gold; some were even thrown back into the rivers.

question: Most white gold rings are not white on their own. They are plated with a thin layer of which rare platinum-group metal to give them their bright finish?
topic: Jewellery
source_excerpt: most will be coated with a very thin layer of rhodium.

extra.why_interesting: Millions of people wear a metal they have never heard of; the brilliant white of a 'white gold' ring is a different, far rarer element on the surface.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's White gold article confirms most white gold is coated with a thin rhodium layer, and rhodium is a rare platinum-group metal.

explanation: White gold is naturally slightly yellowish or grey, so jewellers coat it in rhodium, one of the rarest metals on Earth, which is why white gold rings need re-plating every few years as the layer wears off.

question: The Cullinan, the largest gem-quality rough diamond ever found, was dug up in 1905 and its biggest cut stone is now called the Great Star of Africa. In which country was it found?
topic: Gems
source_excerpt: The Cullinan was found at the Premier No.2 mine in Cullinan, South Africa, on January 26, 1905, by surface manager Frederick Wells.

extra.why_interesting: The biggest gem diamond ever found now sits split across the British Crown Jewels, yet it came out of the ground on another continent; the 'Great Star of Africa' nickname gives an alert player a foothold.
extra.verification_notes: Cullinan was found at the Premier No.2 mine in Cullinan, South Africa in 1905, and it remains the largest gem-quality rough diamond; no newer find has overtaken it.

explanation: The 3,106-carat Cullinan was found at the Premier Mine near Pretoria, and after being cut in Amsterdam its two largest pieces were set in the British Sovereign's Sceptre and Imperial State Crown.

question: By weight, which precious metal makes up almost all of a modern Olympic gold medal?
topic: Jewellery, gems, gold and precious metals
source_excerpt: The silver and gold medals must have a composition of 92.5% silver, and the Olympic gold medal must be plated with at least six grams of fine gold.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the most famous gold object in sport is actually gold. In reality the medal is almost entirely silver with a thin gold coating, so the first- and second-place medals are made of the same main metal.
extra.verification_notes: Olympic gold medals must be at least 92.5% silver with at least 6 g gold plating, so silver is correct (per APMEX; no newer change found).

explanation: Olympic rules require a gold medal to be at least 92.5 percent silver, coated with just 6 grams of gold, so first and second place are basically the same metal with a different finish.

question: Halloumi, the squeaky cheese you can grill without it melting, is the national cheese of which Mediterranean island?
topic: Bread, cheese and dairy around the world
source_excerpt: It is protected as a geographical indication in the European Union, as a protected designation of origin (PDO), which means, within the EU, only products made in certain parts of Cyprus can be called 'halloumi'.

extra.why_interesting: Many players have eaten halloumi dozens of times without ever placing it on a map; the squeaky-grillable clue plus 'Mediterranean island' narrows it to a satisfying click.
extra.verification_notes: Halloumi originates in Cyprus and is EU-protected as a Cypriot PDO; it is widely called Cyprus's national cheese, and nothing newer contradicts this (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halloumi).

explanation: Halloumi has been made on Cyprus for centuries and won EU protected status in 2021. Its high melting point comes from being heated in its own whey during production.

question: Before they go into the oven, traditional bagels are briefly dunked in what to give them their glossy, chewy crust?
topic: Bread, cheese and dairy around the world
source_excerpt: boiling each bagel for 60–90 seconds in water that may contain additives such as lye, baking soda, barley malt syrup, or honey

extra.why_interesting: Most people assume bread only ever meets an oven; the idea of dunking dough in boiling water first is the quiet secret behind the texture everyone recognises.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms bagels are boiled in water (optionally with additives) before baking, which gives the chewy, shiny crust.

explanation: The short boil gelatinises the starch on the surface, so the crust turns shiny and chewy instead of fluffy. Bakers often add a little malt or honey to the water for extra sheen.

question: Skyr, a thick cultured dairy product eaten for over a thousand years and technically classed as a cheese, is the pride of which North Atlantic island nation?
topic: Bread, cheese and dairy around the world
source_excerpt: a traditional Icelandic cultured dairy product

extra.why_interesting: Skyr now sits in supermarket fridges worldwide labelled like yogurt; players are surprised it is technically a cheese and pleased to pin it to its home island.
extra.verification_notes: Skyr is a traditional Icelandic cultured dairy product, classified as a fresh sour milk cheese, per Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skyr).

explanation: Skyr arrived with Norse settlers over a millennium ago and is made by straining skim milk curdled with cultures and a touch of rennet. That rennet is why it technically counts as a soft cheese, not a yogurt.

question: Traditional Irish brown bread uses no yeast at all. Buttermilk reacts with which pantry powder to make the loaf rise?
topic: Bread, cheese and dairy around the world
source_excerpt: The traditional version includes only flour, buttermilk, salt and baking soda.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume all bread needs yeast; the stem hands them 'buttermilk' and 'pantry powder' so they can reason their way to the chemistry even without knowing the bread.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Irish soda bread article confirms the traditional leavening is baking soda (bicarbonate of soda) reacting with buttermilk, with no yeast.

explanation: The acid in buttermilk fizzes with the bicarbonate to release carbon dioxide, so the loaf is mixed and baked within minutes. The method spread in Ireland in the 1800s because it needed no proving time and no oven, just a pot over the fire.

question: Norway's beloved brown cheese, brunost, is sweet and caramel-coloured because it is made mostly by boiling down which by-product of ordinary cheesemaking?
topic: Bread, cheese and dairy around the world
source_excerpt: Brunost is made from whey, milk, and/or cream... The heat turns the milk sugars into caramel, which gives the cheese its characteristic brown colour and sweetness.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture cheese as curds pressed together; brunost is made from the liquid that is normally thrown away, and the caramel colour is the clue that something unusual is happening.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms brunost is made from whey (a cheesemaking by-product), often with milk/cream, boiled until the milk sugars caramelise.

explanation: Hours of simmering caramelise the lactose in the whey, which is where the colour and fudge-like sweetness come from. Norwegians slice it thin onto waffles and bread for breakfast.

question: Before being ground for traditional Mexican tortillas, corn kernels are soaked in water mixed with which alkaline substance, better known from mortar and whitewash?
topic: Bread, cheese and dairy around the world
source_excerpt: The Aztec and Maya civilizations developed nixtamalization by using slaked lime (calcium hydroxide, or 'cal') and lye (potassium hydroxide) to create alkaline solutions.

extra.why_interesting: Nobody expects a building material in their food; the mortar and whitewash hint lets players reason to 'lime' and feel clever rather than lost.
extra.verification_notes: Nixtamalization uses limewater (calcium hydroxide, 'cal'), which is also the lime used in mortar and whitewash; no newer development contradicts this (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nixtamalization).

explanation: The process, called nixtamalization, dates back thousands of years in Mesoamerica. It softens the kernels, frees up the vitamin niacin, and gives tortillas their distinctive flavour.

question: Airag, the lightly alcoholic national drink of Mongolia, is fermented from the milk of which animal?
topic: Bread, cheese and dairy around the world
source_excerpt: a traditional fermented dairy product made from mare milk

extra.why_interesting: Players default to cows, goats or yaks; the answer rewards anyone who knows how central horses are to Mongolian life.
extra.verification_notes: Airag is fermented mare's milk (horse), per Wikipedia; I found no contradicting source or newer development, though I did not check the national-drink or alcohol claims directly.

explanation: Mare's milk is churned in a leather sack for days until it turns fizzy, sour and a few percent alcohol. Ancient Greek writers already described steppe nomads drinking fermented horse milk under the name kumis.

question: Roughly what share of the world's adults have a reduced ability to digest lactose, the sugar in milk?
topic: Bread, cheese and dairy around the world
source_excerpt: Worldwide, around 65% of adults are affected by lactose malabsorption.

extra.why_interesting: Players from dairy-heavy cultures assume lactose intolerance is a minority condition; globally it is the norm, and digesting milk as an adult is the exception.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia reports about 65% of adults worldwide have lactose malabsorption, consistent with 'about two-thirds' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lactose_intolerance).

explanation: Around two in three adults worldwide stop producing much lactase after childhood. Northern Europeans are the outliers, where most adults carry a mutation that keeps the enzyme switched on for life.

question: Sales of which crumbly Yorkshire cheese were rescued in the 1990s after an animated inventor and his dog kept praising it on screen?
topic: Bread, cheese and dairy around the world
source_excerpt: In the 1990s, sales of Wensleydale cheese from the Wensleydale Creamery had fallen so low that production in Wensleydale itself was at risk of being suspended.

extra.why_interesting: A cheese saved by a plasticine inventor is delightful, and the 'inventor and his dog' description lets players recognise Wallace and Gromit and then recall the cheese he kept praising.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Wensleydale sales were at risk in the 1990s and were revived by Wallace & Gromit; the cheese is described as crumbly.

explanation: Wallace of Wallace and Gromit declared his love for it, and the struggling Hawes creamery signed a licensing deal that put the pair on its packaging. Creator Nick Park said he chose the cheese simply because the word was fun for Wallace to say.

question: A regional Italian bank, Credem, keeps vaults filled with ageing wheels of which cheese, accepted from producers as collateral for loans?
topic: Bread, cheese and dairy around the world
source_excerpt: more than half a million wheels of Parmigiano-Reggiano, valued at about 300 million euros, exposed to record temperatures inside the underground vaults of Credito Emiliano Bank (Credem)

extra.why_interesting: Banks taking cheese as security sounds like a joke; the regional name Credem and 'wheels' are the footholds that steer players to the giant cheese of Emilia.
extra.verification_notes: Credem has accepted Parmigiano Reggiano as loan collateral since 1953 and still holds over 500,000 wheels in its vaults as of August 2026 (https://www.euronews.com/business/2026/08/11/extreme-heat-strains-italys-cheese-banks-where-parmigiano-backs-farm-loans).

explanation: Each wheel is worth hundreds of euros and must age for at least a year, so producers borrow against it while the bank's staff turn and brush the wheels in its warehouses. If a loan goes bad, the bank simply sells the cheese.

question: Cows provide roughly four-fifths of the world's milk. Which animal comes a clear second, well ahead of goats and sheep?
topic: Bread, cheese and dairy around the world
source_excerpt: Cattle produce 81 percent of world milk production, followed by buffaloes with 15 percent, goats with 2 percent and sheep with 1 percent

extra.why_interesting: Players almost always guess goat; the real runner-up is the water buffalo, driven by huge herds in India and Pakistan, and the stem explicitly rules out goats and sheep to force genuine knowledge.
extra.verification_notes: FAO data show cattle ~81%, buffalo ~15%, goats ~2%, sheep ~1% of world milk, so water buffalo is a clear second.

explanation: Buffalo supply around one-seventh of all milk on Earth, most of it in India and Pakistan, where it is prized for being far richer in fat than cow's milk. Europe meets it mostly as Italian buffalo mozzarella.

question: True or false: Stilton cheese may legally be produced in the village of Stilton.
topic: Bread, cheese and dairy around the world
source_excerpt: Stilton cheese cannot be made in Stilton village, which gave the cheese its name, because it is not in any of the three permitted counties.

extra.why_interesting: The obvious assumption is that a cheese can of course be made in its namesake village; the legal reality is the exact opposite, which makes the false answer a genuine jolt.
extra.verification_notes: Stilton PDO limits production to Derbyshire, Leicestershire and Nottinghamshire; Stilton village (Cambridgeshire) is excluded, and a 2013 bid to change that was rejected by Defra.

explanation: Protected status limits Stilton to three English counties, and the village of Stilton sits in a fourth, Cambridgeshire. The village got its name on the cheese because an 18th-century coaching inn there sold it to travellers, not because it was made there.

question: Which famous English blue cheese is legally forbidden from being made in the village it is named after?
topic: Bread, cheese and dairy around the world
source_excerpt: Stilton cheese cannot be made in Stilton village, which gave the cheese its name, because it is not in any of the three permitted counties

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a place-named cheese must come from that place, like Cheddar or Gouda. Stilton flips it: the law bans the cheese from its own namesake village, which was only ever the coaching inn where it was sold, not made.
extra.verification_notes: Stilton PDO restricts production to Derbyshire, Leicestershire and Nottinghamshire, so the Cambridgeshire village can't make it; the 2013 bid to change this was rejected.

explanation: The village of Stilton is in Cambridgeshire, but the protected designation only allows the cheese to be made in Derbyshire, Leicestershire and Nottinghamshire. The village was merely the coaching stop where the cheese was sold to travellers.

question: The magician David Copperfield borrowed his stage name from a novel by which author?
topic: Famous illusionists
source_excerpt: he adopted the stage name David Copperfield, taken from the Charles Dickens novel, because he liked its sound.

extra.why_interesting: Players know the magician's name so well they rarely notice it is a borrowed literary title; the answer makes the connection click instantly.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Kotkin adopted the name David Copperfield from the Charles Dickens novel.

explanation: He was born David Kotkin and took the name of the Dickens novel as a teenager. The real David Copperfield never made the Statue of Liberty disappear.

question: In the 2017 musical film The Greatest Showman, Hugh Jackman plays which real 19th-century circus impresario?
topic: Circus
source_excerpt: a heavily fictionalized depiction of the life of P. T. Barnum, a showman and entertainer who created the Barnum & Bailey Circus.

extra.why_interesting: A hugely popular film with a real historical showman behind it; players who know the songs may not realise the hero was a real circus founder.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Hugh Jackman portrays P. T. Barnum in the 2017 film The Greatest Showman.

explanation: Phineas Taylor Barnum's travelling show later merged into Ringling Bros. and Barnum and Bailey, billed as the Greatest Show on Earth.

question: In 1974 the French high-wire artist Philippe Petit walked a cable illegally rigged between which two New York buildings?
topic: Circus
source_excerpt: Petit's most famous performance was in August 1974, conducted on a wire between the roofs of the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center in Lower Manhattan

extra.why_interesting: The feat sounds impossible and illegal, and it was both; the buildings themselves add an emotional jolt.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Petit's unauthorized August 1974 wire walk between the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center; nothing found that supersedes it.

explanation: He spent about 45 minutes on the wire 400 metres above the street and was arrested when he stepped off. The documentary Man on Wire later won an Oscar.

question: Penn Jillette's famously silent stage partner legally changed his name to a single word. What is it?
topic: Famous illusionists
source_excerpt: Teller legally changed his name to the mononym Teller, his family surname.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the one-word name is a stage gimmick; it is actually his full legal name.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Teller legally changed his name to the mononym 'Teller' and is famously silent on stage; no newer events found that change this.

explanation: He was born Raymond Joseph Teller and dropped everything but the surname, so even his passport says just Teller.

question: The founder of which circus company paid for a seat on a Soyuz rocket and visited the International Space Station in 2009?
topic: Circus
source_excerpt: In September 2009, Laliberté became the first Canadian space tourist. He launched on the Soyuz TMA-16 spacecraft

extra.why_interesting: A former street fire-eater becoming rich enough to buy a seat on a Soyuz rocket is a surprising arc, and the company is deducible as the one circus brand wealthy enough.
extra.verification_notes: Guy Laliberté, co-founder of Cirque du Soleil, flew to the ISS on Soyuz TMA-16 in September 2009 as a space tourist (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guy_Laliberté).

explanation: Guy Laliberté started out as a fire-eater and stilt-walker in Quebec before building Cirque du Soleil into a global brand. His ticket reportedly cost around 35 million dollars.

question: In 2003 David Blaine spent 44 days without food in a transparent box hanging above a riverbank in which city?
topic: Famous illusionists
source_excerpt: Suspended 30 feet in the air next to Potters Fields Park on the south bank of the River Thames in London

extra.why_interesting: Players picture Blaine as a New York street magician, yet his most notorious endurance stunt took place abroad in front of jeering crowds.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the 2003 'Above the Below' 44-day fast in a box beside the Thames at Potters Fields, London.

explanation: The box hung beside the Thames near Tower Bridge, and locals famously threw eggs and flew burgers up to him on remote-controlled helicopters.

question: The modern circus began in London in 1768 as a show built around tricks performed on which animal?
topic: Circus
source_excerpt: began performing exhibitions of trick horse riding

extra.why_interesting: Players picture clowns and trapeze as the heart of the circus, but the whole form and even the round ring exist because of one animal.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia credits Philip Astley with founding the modern circus in London in 1768 with trick horse riding shows.

explanation: Philip Astley was a former cavalryman who did stunt riding, and the circular ring of roughly 13 metres was the size that let a horse gallop steadily while he stood on its back. Clowns and acrobats were only added to fill the gaps between rides.

question: After 146 years, the Ringling Bros. and Barnum and Bailey Circus gave what was announced as its final performance in which year?
topic: Circus
source_excerpt: After 146 Years, Ringling Bros. And Barnum & Bailey Circus To Shut Down

extra.why_interesting: Players know the famous American circus closed but tend to place it either in the distant past or very recently; the elephant-ban era pins it down.
extra.verification_notes: The circus announced in Jan 2017 it would close after 146 years and held its final show on May 21, 2017; the 2023 relaunch doesn't change that, given the 'announced as' wording (https://www.npr.org/sections/thetwo-way/2017/01/15/509903805/after-146-years-ringling-bros-and-barnum-bailey-circus-to-shut-down).

explanation: Falling ticket sales after the circus retired its elephants in 2016 ended the Greatest Show on Earth the following spring. The brand relaunched in 2023 without any animals.

question: Which of these magicians performed under the name that was on his birth certificate?
topic: Famous illusionists
source_excerpt: Penn Fraser Jillette (born March 5, 1955) is an American magician, entertainer and author.

extra.why_interesting: The most unusual-sounding name in the list is the only genuine one; players have to know the others are invented.
extra.verification_notes: Penn Fraser Jillette is his birth name; Angel (Sarantakos), Dynamo (Steven Frayne) and Houdini (Erik Weisz) used stage names.

explanation: Penn Fraser Jillette is his real name, while Criss Angel was born Christopher Sarantakos, Dynamo is Steven Frayne, and Houdini was born Erik Weisz in Budapest.

question: Houdini's friendship with which famous author collapsed because the writer believed in séances and spirit contact, which Houdini spent his later years debunking?
topic: Famous illusionists
source_excerpt: compromised Houdini's friendship with Sir Arthur Conan Doyle

extra.why_interesting: The creator of the most rational detective in fiction was a devout believer in séances, and the professional trickster was the sceptic.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Houdini's anti-spiritualist crusade ended his friendship with Arthur Conan Doyle, a committed spiritualist.

explanation: The creator of Sherlock Holmes was convinced Houdini had genuine supernatural powers, and the two fell out after a séance in which Doyle's wife claimed to channel Houdini's mother.

question: The magician Chung Ling Soo died on a London stage in 1918 when which notoriously dangerous trick went wrong?
alternative_answers: Catching a bullet in his teeth
topic: Famous illusionists
source_excerpt: Condemned to Death by the Boxers... Wood Green Empire in London... live bullet into his lung... inquest ruled his death 'accidental' with a final verdict of 'misadventure.'

extra.why_interesting: The stem's 'died on stage' invites players to reason toward the one trick with a genuine body count, and the double surprise is that the Chinese mystic was an American in disguise.
extra.verification_notes: Chung Ling Soo was fatally shot during his bullet catch trick at the Wood Green Empire, London, in March 1918 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chung_Ling_Soo); he died in hospital the next day, so 'died on a stage' is loose wording.

explanation: A worn gun fired a real bullet into his chest, and the audience heard him speak English for the first time. He was actually William Robinson from New York, who had posed as Chinese for nearly twenty years.

question: In 1983, David Copperfield stunned a TV audience by making which world-famous monument disappear?
topic: Magic and famous illusionists
source_excerpt: the space where the Statue of Liberty once stood was empty.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture stage magic as a card trick or a vanishing assistant; the answer is a 93-metre national monument, which still feels absurd decades later.
extra.verification_notes: Copperfield's TV special 'The Statue of Liberty Disappears' aired April 8, 1983, per Wikipedia.

explanation: The live audience sat on a slowly rotating platform, so when the curtain dropped the statue was simply hidden behind a lighting tower while the view looked unchanged.

question: Harry Houdini built his stage name on the surname of an earlier conjuror known as the father of modern magic. From which country did that magician come?
topic: Magic and famous illusionists
source_excerpt: after reading his autobiography in 1890, Weiss adopted the stage name of 'Houdini' in honour of Robert-Houdin.

extra.why_interesting: Houdini sounds like an invented, almost Italian-flavoured name; the surprise is that it is a borrowed surname with an added letter, honouring an earlier magician from France.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Robert-Houdin was a French magician called the father of modern magic, and that Houdini took his stage name from him.

explanation: He borrowed the name of Jean-Eugène Robert-Houdin, a Parisian clockmaker turned illusionist, and simply added an i, wrongly believing it meant 'like Houdin' in French.

question: Harry Houdini was born Erik Weisz in Budapest. The stage name that made him world-famous was a tribute to a 19th-century magician from which country?
topic: Circus, magic and famous illusionists
source_excerpt: began calling himself 'Harry Houdini' after the French magician Jean-Eugène Robert-Houdin, whose autobiography he read in 1890.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume 'Houdini' is simply the escape artist's own surname, or at least Hungarian like him; in fact it is a borrowed tribute to a Frenchman who died before Houdini was born.
extra.verification_notes: Houdini took his stage name from French magician Jean-Eugène Robert-Houdin, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Houdini; the Kellar tribute applies only to 'Harry', not the surname the question is about.

explanation: The young Weisz idolised Jean-Eugène Robert-Houdin, the French watchmaker turned conjuror often called the father of modern magic, and simply added an 'i' to his hero's name.

question: Which alcoholic drink, one of the oldest known, is made by fermenting honey with water?
topic: Bees, honey and pollination
source_excerpt: Mead...is an alcoholic beverage made by fermenting honey mixed with water

extra.why_interesting: Players think of beer and wine as the ancient drinks; the honey drink is older than most and still made across Central Europe.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia defines mead as an alcoholic beverage made by fermenting honey with water and calls it possibly the most ancient alcoholic drink.

explanation: Mead is made simply by letting yeast ferment diluted honey, and it was being drunk long before grapes were pressed into wine across much of Europe.

question: Any female honey bee larva can become a queen. What must the workers feed it exclusively to make that happen?
topic: Bees, honey and pollination
source_excerpt: queen larvae continue to be fed this special substance throughout their development.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a queen is born special; in fact any female larva can become queen, and diet alone decides it.
extra.verification_notes: Queen larvae are fed royal jelly throughout development, which is the standard answer; the mechanism has some nuance but nothing contradicts it (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_jelly).

explanation: Royal jelly is a secretion from glands in young worker bees' heads, and a larva raised on nothing else grows into a fertile queen instead of a worker.

question: A male honey bee has a grandfather but no father. What is special about the egg he hatches from?
topic: Bees, honey and pollination
source_excerpt: a male has no father and cannot have sons, but he has a grandfather and can have grandsons.

extra.why_interesting: A creature with a grandfather but no father sounds impossible until you realise the queen lays some eggs without mating them.
extra.verification_notes: Haplodiploidy: drones develop from unfertilised eggs, so they have no father but do have a maternal grandfather (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haplodiploidy).

explanation: The queen lays male eggs without any sperm, so a drone carries only his mother's genes, while his mother of course had a father.

question: A returning honey bee's waggle dance tells her sisters which way to fly. The angle of the dance gives the direction of the flowers relative to what?
topic: Bees, honey and pollination
source_excerpt: any angle to the right or left of the sun is coded by a corresponding angle to the right or left of the upward direction.

extra.why_interesting: Players know bees dance, but not that the dance is a map drawn against a landmark in the sky.
extra.verification_notes: Waggle run angle from vertical encodes the flower direction relative to the sun's azimuth, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waggle_dance.

explanation: Dancing straight up the comb means fly towards the sun, and every degree off vertical means the same degree off the sun's position, a code Karl von Frisch cracked on his way to a Nobel Prize.

question: Honey bees are useless for tomato flowers, which only release pollen when shaken. Which bees do greenhouse growers buy in cardboard boxes to do the job?
topic: Bees, honey and pollination
source_excerpt: Honeybees cannot perform buzz pollination.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume honey bees are the universal pollinator; tomato growers actually have to buy a different bee by the box.
extra.verification_notes: Honey bees cannot buzz-pollinate, and greenhouse tomato growers buy commercial bumblebee colonies in cardboard boxes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzz_pollination).

explanation: A bumblebee grabs the flower and vibrates its flight muscles to shake the pollen loose, a trick called buzz pollination that honey bees simply cannot perform.

question: World Bee Day falls on 20 May, the birthday of an 18th-century beekeeping pioneer. Which small European country proposed the day to the United Nations?
topic: Bees, honey and pollination
source_excerpt: Slovenia proposed the establishment of World Bee Day. The UN Member States approved Slovenia's proposal in December 2017.

extra.why_interesting: Players expect a big agricultural nation behind a UN day; it was a small Alpine country where beekeeping is a national passion.
extra.verification_notes: Slovenia proposed World Bee Day and the UN approved it in Dec 2017; 20 May is Anton Janša's commemorated birth/baptism date, so the 'birthday' wording is a minor quibble.

explanation: Slovenia has one of the highest numbers of beekeepers per head in the world, and the date honours Anton Janša, who taught beekeeping at the Habsburg court in Vienna.

question: Which flavouring, grown mainly in Madagascar, must be pollinated flower by flower by hand because the only bee that does it naturally lives in Mexico?
topic: Bees, honey and pollination
source_excerpt: all vanilla grown today is pollinated by hand

extra.why_interesting: A flavour in every kitchen depends on workers touching each flower by hand, because the right bee stayed home in Mexico.
extra.verification_notes: Vanilla is unambiguous: Madagascar is the top producer and all commercial vanilla is hand-pollinated. The 'only bee in Mexico' detail is a simplification, since Wikipedia says the Melipona claim is unsubstantiated and names Eulaema orchid bees instead.

explanation: The vanilla orchid is native to Mexico, and when it was taken to the Indian Ocean islands its bee did not come along, so a twelve-year-old enslaved boy named Edmond Albius worked out the hand method in 1841.

question: When Queen Elizabeth II died in 2022, the royal beekeeper went to the Buckingham Palace hives, knocked gently and did something a centuries-old custom demands. What did he do?
alternative_answers: Informed the bees of her death
Announced her death to the bees
Told them the Queen had died
topic: Bees, honey and pollination
source_excerpt: Chapple travelled to both locations to carry on the ritual that apparently dates back centuries. He gave a gentle rap on each hive's side

extra.why_interesting: Players picture a modern state funeral; the detail that someone formally informed the bees is folk magic surviving at the heart of the monarchy.
extra.verification_notes: Royal beekeeper John Chapple knocked on the hives and told the bees of the Queen's death, per the centuries-old 'telling the bees' custom (https://www.cbc.ca/lite/story/1.6582883).

explanation: The old European custom of telling the bees holds that hives must be informed of a death in the household, or the bees will leave or die, so he announced that their mistress was dead and they now had a new master.

question: A worker honey bee lives about six weeks in summer. Roughly how much honey does one worker make in her whole life?
topic: Bees, honey and pollination
source_excerpt: A worker bee gathers in her entire life 0.8 gram (0.0288 ounce) of honey.

extra.why_interesting: Players imagine a busy bee filling at least a small jar; the real figure is so tiny that every spoonful represents dozens of bee lifetimes.
extra.verification_notes: Multiple sources (e.g. Canadian Honey Council, https://honeycouncil.ca/industry-overview/bee-facts/) say a worker makes under a teaspoon (~1/12 tsp, 0.8 g) of honey in her lifetime.

explanation: One worker makes only about a twelfth of a teaspoon, so a single 500 gram jar represents the entire working lives of well over a thousand bees.

question: True or false: honey bees were buzzing across North America long before the first Europeans arrived.
topic: Bees, honey and pollination
source_excerpt: Humans are responsible for its considerable additional range, introducing European subspecies into North America (early 1600s)

extra.why_interesting: Players assume honey bees are everywhere by nature; in fact they crossed the Atlantic in ships, and some Native Americans called them the white man's flies.
extra.verification_notes: Honey bees (Apis mellifera) are not native to the Americas and were introduced by Europeans in the early 1600s, so 'False' is correct (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_honey_bee).

explanation: The honey bee is a European and African species that colonists shipped to Virginia in the 1620s, and it then spread westward across the continent ahead of the settlers themselves.

question: In Turkey's Black Sea mountains, bees feeding on rhododendron make a honey that leaves people dizzy, hallucinating and sometimes hospitalised. By what two-word nickname is it known?
topic: Bees, honey and pollination
source_excerpt: Mad honey is honey that contains grayanotoxins

extra.why_interesting: Honey is the picture of wholesome; a honey that makes people hallucinate and collapse, and has done since antiquity, overturns that.
extra.verification_notes: Mad honey is the standard English name for grayanotoxin-containing rhododendron honey from Turkey's Black Sea region (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mad_honey).

explanation: The culprit is grayanotoxin from the rhododendron nectar, and the Greek general Xenophon described his whole army collapsing after eating it near Trabzon in 401 BC.

question: In 2012, beekeepers in Alsace were alarmed to find their bees producing bright blue and green honey. The bees had been feasting on waste from a factory making which famous sweets?
topic: Bees, honey and pollination
source_excerpt: bees tempted over to the biogas plant for sugary snacks; the plant processes waste for confectionary giant Mars, which makes M&M's

extra.why_interesting: Blue honey sounds like a hoax; the explanation is a bee shortcut to the sweetest source around, a candy factory's leftovers.
extra.verification_notes: Multiple 2012 reports confirm Alsace bees near Ribeauvillé made blue/green honey from waste M&M's at a biogas plant processing Mars factory waste (https://www.france24.com/en/20121004-mms-crazed-french-bees-produce-blue-green-honey-ribeauville-alsace-france).

explanation: A biogas plant was processing coloured sugar residue from the nearby Mars factory, and the bees preferred that easy sugar to flowers, turning out honey in candy-shell colours that could not legally be sold.

question: Which member of a honeybee colony has a grandfather but no father?
topic: Bees, honey and pollination
source_excerpt: Because the male bee technically has only a mother, and no father, their genealogical tree is unusual.

extra.why_interesting: The stem sounds like a logic trick that cannot be true of any animal; the player who knows that bee sex is decided by whether an egg was fertilised gets the satisfying click that it is simply biology.
extra.verification_notes: Drones develop from unfertilized eggs, so they have a mother and maternal grandfather but no father; queens and workers have fathers (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drone_(bee)).

explanation: Male bees hatch from eggs the queen never fertilised, so they have no father. The queen herself came from a fertilised egg, so every drone still has a grandfather on his mother's side.

question: A single ice crystal is transparent, and a block of pure ice is nearly clear. So why does a field of fresh snow look brilliantly white?
correct_answer: Light scatters off countless crystal surfaces
alternative_answers: The many crystal surfaces reflect light in all directions
Multiple reflections scatter all colours equally
Air pockets and crystal faces bounce the light around
Same reason crushed glass or foam looks white
It reflects every colour of light, which adds up to white
headline_answer: Light scatters off countless crystal surfaces
topic: Ice, snow and the polar regions
source_excerpt: Although the ice is clear, scattering of light by the crystal facets and hollows/imperfections mean that the crystals often appear white in color due to diffuse reflection

extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Snow article attributes the white appearance to scattering of light by crystal facets and imperfections, which matches the claimed answer.

explanation: Snow is made of millions of tiny ice crystals packed loosely with air between them. Each crystal is clear, but every surface and every air gap bends or reflects a little of the light that hits it. After bouncing between thousands of surfaces, the light is scattered back out in all directions. Because ice reflects all visible colours roughly equally, the scattered light contains the full spectrum, and our eyes see that as white. The same thing happens with crushed glass, sea foam or a shattered windscreen: a transparent material turns white as soon as it is broken into many small pieces. Old, compressed glacier ice has had the air squeezed out, so it lets light pass deeper and absorbs the red end of the spectrum, which is why it looks blue instead.

question: Deserts are defined by how little precipitation falls, not by heat. Which continent is Earth's largest desert?
topic: Ice, snow and the polar regions
source_excerpt: Deserts generally receive less than 250 mm (10 in) of precipitation each year.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture deserts as hot sand; the answer flips that image onto a continent buried in ice.
extra.verification_notes: Antarctica (about 14.2 million km²) is listed as the largest desert, and deserts are defined by low precipitation, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desert.

explanation: Its interior gets only a few centimetres of precipitation a year, far drier than the Sahara, so the whole frozen continent counts as one enormous desert.

question: Stand exactly at the North Pole and drill straight down. After a few metres of ice, what do you break into?
topic: Ice, snow and the polar regions
source_excerpt: The sea ice at the North Pole is typically around 2 to 3 m (6 ft 7 in to 9 ft 10 in) thick

extra.why_interesting: Many assume both poles sit on land like Antarctica; the drilling image makes the absence of land vivid.
extra.verification_notes: The North Pole lies on drifting sea ice a few metres thick over the deep Arctic Ocean, so drilling through breaks into the ocean (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Pole).

explanation: There is no land at the North Pole at all, just sea ice a few metres thick floating on an ocean about four kilometres deep.

question: If every bit of ice on Greenland melted, roughly how much would global sea level rise?
topic: Ice, snow and the polar regions
source_excerpt: If the Greenland Ice Sheet melted entirely, scientists estimate that sea level would rise about 7.4 meters (23 feet).

extra.why_interesting: Players know Greenland matters for sea level but rarely know whether it means centimetres or tens of metres; the buckets force a real estimate.
extra.verification_notes: Greenland's ice sheet holds about 7.4 m of sea-level equivalent, so 'about 7 metres' is correct and the other options are far off (https://nsidc.org/learn/parts-cryosphere/ice-sheets/why-ice-sheets-matter).

explanation: Greenland alone holds enough ice for about seven metres of sea-level rise, and Antarctica holds enough for roughly 58 metres more.

question: The Antarctic Treaty reserved an entire continent for peace and science and banned military activity there. In which year was it signed?
topic: Ice, snow and the polar regions
source_excerpt: opened for signature on 1 December 1959, and officially entered into force on 23 June 1961.

extra.why_interesting: A Cold War agreement that still works feels like it should be more recent; the actual date surprises players who guess the 1970s.
extra.verification_notes: The Antarctic Treaty was opened for signature on 1 December 1959 and bans military activity; no newer events change this (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctic_Treaty_System).

explanation: Twelve countries signed it in Washington in December 1959, at the height of the Cold War, and it remains in force today with more than fifty parties.

question: An emperor penguin egg must never touch the Antarctic ice during its two months of incubation. Where exactly is it kept?
alternative_answers: On the feet of the male penguin
topic: Ice, snow and the polar regions
source_excerpt: There he balances it on the tops of his feet, engulfing it with loose skin and feathers for around 65–75 days until hatching.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a nest or the mother; the answer is a fasting father balancing the egg on his toes in the polar night.
extra.verification_notes: Emperor penguin males incubate the egg on the tops of their feet under a brood fold for ~65-75 days, per Wikipedia.

explanation: The male balances it on his feet under a warm fold of belly skin through the polar winter, fasting for around two months while the female is away feeding at sea.

question: The word Arctic comes from the ancient Greek name for an animal, not a polar one, but one that shines in the northern night sky. Which animal?
topic: Ice, snow and the polar regions
source_excerpt: derives from the Greek word ἀρκτικός (arktikos), meaning 'near the Bear, northern'

extra.why_interesting: Players jump to polar bears, but the real bear is a constellation, and the twist is that the south is literally named as the land without the bear.
extra.verification_notes: Arctic derives from Greek arktikos, 'near the Bear', from arktos 'bear', referring to the constellations Ursa Major/Minor.

explanation: The Greeks named the north after the constellation of the Great Bear, so Antarctic literally means opposite the bear, which fits nicely, since no polar bear has ever lived there.

question: Nicknamed the Doomsday Vault, a backup store of seeds from the world's crops is tunnelled into a permafrost mountainside on which Norwegian Arctic archipelago?
topic: Ice, snow and the polar regions
source_excerpt: The facility is situated on Spitsbergen Island within the Svalbard archipelago... vault entrance is 130 m (430 ft) inside a sandstone mountain.

extra.why_interesting: The Doomsday Vault nickname is widely known, but players have to place it on the map, and the permafrost detail explains why it is there.
extra.verification_notes: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault, nicknamed the Doomsday Vault, is on Spitsbergen in the Svalbard archipelago and remains operational.

explanation: Opened in 2008 near Longyearbyen, it relies on the permafrost to keep the seeds frozen even if the power fails, and holds over a million seed samples.

question: Polar bear fur is not actually white. Each hair is hollow and transparent. What colour is the skin underneath?
topic: Ice, snow and the polar regions
source_excerpt: The skin, including the nose and lips, is black and absorbs heat.

extra.why_interesting: Everything about a polar bear reads white, so a black skin feels wrong until the player remembers it needs to soak up heat.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms polar bear guard hairs are hollow and transparent and the skin is black (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_bear).

explanation: The dark skin helps absorb warmth, while the clear hairs scatter light so the whole animal appears white against the snow.

question: Beneath almost four kilometres of Antarctic ice lies a liquid freshwater lake about the size of Lake Ontario. It shares its name with the Russian station above it, where the coldest air temperature on Earth was recorded. What is the name?
topic: Ice, snow and the polar regions
source_excerpt: The coldest naturally occurring temperature ever observed on Earth, −89 °C (−128 °F), was recorded at Vostok Station on 21 July 1983.

extra.why_interesting: Liquid water under four kilometres of ice at the coldest place on Earth is a shock; the station name gives knowledgeable players a route in.
extra.verification_notes: Lake Vostok is subglacial freshwater under ~4 km of ice, named for Vostok Station, which recorded the −89 °C world low; the Lake Ontario comparison is loose but acceptable.

explanation: The lake has been sealed under the ice for millions of years, while the station above recorded minus 89 degrees Celsius in 1983, still the lowest air temperature ever measured at ground level.

question: The world's southernmost active volcano, standing near the main American and New Zealand bases in Antarctica, holds a rare permanent lava lake in its crater. Name it.
topic: Ice, snow and the polar regions
source_excerpt: Mount Erebus is the southernmost active volcano on Earth.

extra.why_interesting: A permanently molten lava lake on the frozen continent is a wonderful contradiction, and the Greek underworld name rewards players who know it.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Erebus is the southernmost active volcano, with a persistent lava lake, near McMurdo Station and Scott Base; I found no newer event that changes this.

explanation: Erebus rises almost 3,800 metres above Ross Island, and its summit crater has held a churning lake of molten rock for decades, one of only a handful on Earth.

question: Nobody lives in Antarctica permanently, but researchers and support staff come and go. At the busiest point of the summer season, roughly how many people are on the whole continent?
topic: Ice, snow and the polar regions
source_excerpt: During the summer months, about 5,000 people reside at research stations

extra.why_interesting: A continent the size of Europe and the United States combined with only a few thousand people on it at its busiest overturns any sense of scale.
