extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia gives about 5,000 people at research stations in summer (about 1,000 in winter), consistent with 'a few thousand'; tourists arrive in waves and don't push the simultaneous peak into the tens of thousands.

explanation: The summer peak is only around four to five thousand people spread across a continent bigger than Europe, and in winter that falls to about a thousand.

question: Penguins are Southern Hemisphere birds, yet one species lives naturally on the equator, with some colonies just north of it. On which islands?
topic: Ice, snow and the polar regions
source_excerpt: The northern tip of Isabela crosses the equator, meaning that some Galápagos penguins live in the Northern Hemisphere, the only penguins to do so.

extra.why_interesting: Penguins mean ice to most players; a penguin on the equator is a delightful exception, and the islands' fame makes it reachable.
extra.verification_notes: Galápagos penguins live on the equator, with some on northern Isabela in the Northern Hemisphere, and no other penguin species does; source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gal%C3%A1pagos_penguin

explanation: The Galápagos penguin survives there thanks to the cold Humboldt and Cromwell currents, making it the only penguin found naturally north of the equator.

question: The permanent American research station at the geographic South Pole is named after two explorers: the man who reached the pole first in 1911 and the rival who arrived about a month later. Name them both.
alternative_answers: Roald Amundsen and Robert Falcon Scott
topic: Ice, snow and the polar regions
source_excerpt: leaders of the competing first and second expeditions to reach the pole

extra.why_interesting: The month-later clue tells the whole tragic story of the race in one line, and the station name honours both the winner and the loser.
extra.verification_notes: Station is still named Amundsen–Scott South Pole Station for Amundsen (Dec 1911) and Scott (Jan 1912), per Wikipedia; no renaming found.

explanation: Roald Amundsen's Norwegian team arrived in December 1911 on skis with dog sleds, while Robert Falcon Scott's British party got there in January 1912 and died on the way back.

question: Antarctica's largest ice shelf is a floating slab of ice roughly the size of France. It takes its name from the British naval explorer who reached it in 1841. What is the surname?
topic: Ice, snow and the polar regions
source_excerpt: the largest ice shelf of Antarctica

extra.why_interesting: A floating slab of ice the size of France is hard to picture, and the 1841 date plus the naval clue gives polar-history fans a fair shot at the surname.
extra.verification_notes: Ross Ice Shelf is Antarctica's largest, about the size of France, named for James Clark Ross who found it in 1841 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Ice_Shelf).

explanation: James Clark Ross sailed along its towering ice cliffs in 1841, and his name now covers the shelf, the sea beside it and the island nearby.

question: Which country prints the Latin word 'Helvetia' on its postage stamps instead of its own name?
topic: Post, stamps and communication before the internet
source_excerpt: Swiss stamps are inscribed with the word Helvetia, rather than 'Schweiz', 'Suisse' 'Svizzera', or 'Svizra'.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume every stamp names its country plainly; Switzerland dodges its four-language problem with a Latin word from Roman times.
extra.verification_notes: Swiss stamps are inscribed 'Helvetia' rather than Schweiz/Suisse/Svizzera/Svizra, and the practice continues today.

explanation: With four official languages, Switzerland sidestepped the argument by using the Latin name of the Roman-era region, and it still appears on coins and stamps today.

question: True or false: the distress signal SOS was chosen because it abbreviates 'Save Our Souls'.
topic: Post, stamps and communication before the internet
source_excerpt: SOS, when it was first agreed upon by the International Radio Telegraphic Convention in 1906, was merely a distinctive Morse code sequence and was initially not an abbreviation.

extra.why_interesting: Almost everyone 'knows' it means Save Our Souls; the truth is it means nothing at all and was picked for its rhythm.
extra.verification_notes: SOS was chosen as a distinctive Morse sequence, not an abbreviation; 'Save Our Souls' is a later backronym (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SOS).

explanation: SOS stands for nothing; it was adopted in 1906 because three dots, three dashes, three dots is easy to send and impossible to mistake in Morse code. 'Save Our Souls' was invented afterwards as a memory aid.

question: The legendary Pony Express shut down in October 1861, just two days after which new technology linked the two coasts of the United States?
topic: Post, stamps and communication before the internet
source_excerpt: The Pony Express announced its closure on October 26, 1861, two days after the transcontinental telegraph reached Salt Lake City and connected Omaha, Nebraska, and Sacramento.

extra.why_interesting: The Pony Express feels like a decades-long Wild West institution; it actually lasted about 18 months and was killed almost overnight by a wire.
extra.verification_notes: Transcontinental telegraph completed Oct 24, 1861; Pony Express announced closure Oct 26, 1861 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pony_Express).

explanation: The transcontinental telegraph line was completed on 24 October 1861, and a service that took ten days on horseback could not compete with messages arriving in minutes. The Pony Express had run for only about eighteen months.

question: The 'Inverted Jenny' of 1918 is the most famous misprinted stamp in American history. What is shown upside down on it?
topic: Post, stamps and communication before the internet
source_excerpt: the image of the Curtiss JN-4 airplane in the center of the design is printed upside-down.

extra.why_interesting: A printing mistake that would get a worker fired turned a 24-cent stamp into one of the most valuable collectibles in America.
extra.verification_notes: The Curtiss JN-4 airplane is printed upside down on the Inverted Jenny, per Wikipedia; no newer developments affect this.

explanation: It was the first US airmail stamp, and the Curtiss 'Jenny' biplane in the middle came out flying belly-up on a single sheet of a hundred. Each one is now worth well over a million dollars.

question: In 1850, before founding his famous news agency, Paul Julius Reuter sent stock prices between Aachen and Brussels faster than the train by using what?
topic: Post, stamps and communication before the internet
source_excerpt: Until the entire distance was connected by telegraph, messages were transferred on the leg between Brussels and Aachen using homing pigeons

extra.why_interesting: A global news giant that today moves data at light speed got its start with birds beating the train by hours.
extra.verification_notes: Reuter used homing pigeons between Brussels and Aachen to bridge the telegraph gap, per Wikipedia; the 1850 date and 'faster than the train' detail were not confirmed on that page.

explanation: The telegraph lines from Berlin and Paris did not yet meet, so Reuter's pigeons covered the gap in about two hours, beating the railway by several hours.

question: In which decade was the first machine for sending images over a wire, the ancestor of the fax, patented?
topic: Post, stamps and communication before the internet
source_excerpt: He received British patent 9745 on May 27, 1843, for his 'Electric Printing Telegraph.'

extra.why_interesting: Players place the fax in the office age of the 1970s or at best the early 20th century; it predates the telephone, the light bulb and the US Civil War.
extra.verification_notes: Alexander Bain's 1843 British patent 9745 is widely cited as the first fax-type patent, so the 1840s answer holds (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fax).

explanation: Alexander Bain patented his 'electric printing telegraph' in 1843, more than thirty years before the telephone existed. Fax technology is older than the light bulb.

question: Britain's post boxes are famously red, but what colour were the first ones painted when they appeared in the 1850s?
topic: Post, stamps and communication before the internet
source_excerpt: made of cast iron, about 1.5 metres high, octagonal in design and painted olive green.

extra.why_interesting: The red British post box is a national icon; the surprise is it started life in a colour chosen to blend in, which worked too well.
extra.verification_notes: Early 1850s British pillar boxes were painted green (olive, then bronze green from 1859) and only repainted red from 1874, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pillar_box.

explanation: The early boxes were a discreet bronze-green, and the Post Office found people simply could not find them. Red was adopted nationwide from 1874 so letters would actually get posted.

question: Which country's state telegram service, used for over 160 years, sent its last telegrams in July 2013, long after most of the world had given them up?
topic: Post, stamps and communication before the internet
source_excerpt: The service was the last large-scale telegram service operating in the world and ceased on 15 July, 2013.

extra.why_interesting: Players think telegrams died with the Beatles; in one giant country people were still queuing to send them in the smartphone era.
extra.verification_notes: BSNL ended India's state telegram service on 15 July 2013 after ~160 years; no later revival found (https://www.cnn.com/2013/07/15/world/asia/last-telegram-india/index.html).

explanation: Crowds queued at telegraph offices on the final day to send farewell telegrams as souvenirs. Western Union in the US had sent its last one back in 2006.

question: In 1973 the Himalayan kingdom of Bhutan issued stamps that could be played on which household device?
topic: Post, stamps and communication before the internet
source_excerpt: each stamp being a plastic record that can be played on a phonograph

extra.why_interesting: A stamp is paper and glue in everyone's head; a tiny Himalayan kingdom made ones you could play like a single.
extra.verification_notes: Bhutan's 1973 talking stamps were miniature vinyl records playable on a standard phonograph/record player, per https://www.linns.com/news/us-stamps-postal-history/tip-of-the-week--bhutan-1973-phonograph-record-set.html

explanation: The stamps were miniature vinyl records with sticky backs, playing the national anthem and folk songs on an ordinary turntable. Bhutan used novelty stamps like these as a major export earner.

question: Which noble family ran the imperial postal service of the Holy Roman Empire as a private business for more than three hundred years?
topic: Post, stamps and communication before the internet
source_excerpt: The Thurn-und-Taxis Post was operated by the Princely House of Thurn and Taxis between 1806 and 1867.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture post as a state job; in central Europe for 300 years it was a private family business that made one dynasty fabulously rich.
extra.verification_notes: Thurn und Taxis is the clearly correct family; the 300+ years figure is loose (about 1490 to 1867 overall, 1615 to 1806 as hereditary imperial office) but defensible. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thurn-und-Taxis_Post

explanation: Starting in the 1490s, the family built relay routes from Brussels to Innsbruck and beyond, and the postal monopoly made them princes. The last of their postal rights were bought out by Prussia in 1867.

question: A 1918 American airmail stamp showing a biplane is one of the most valuable stamps in the world, with single copies selling for over a million dollars. Only one sheet of a hundred escaped the printers with the error that made it famous. What was wrong with the plane?
topic: Post, stamps and communication before the internet
source_excerpt: The image of the Curtiss JN-4 airplane in the center of the design is printed upside-down; it is one of the most famous errors in American philately.

extra.why_interesting: A mistake that would get a printer fired became one of the most valuable objects you can fit in an envelope. The stem gives the player enough to deduce the famous error.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the 1918 Inverted Jenny's Curtiss JN-4 biplane was printed upside down, only one pane of 100 escaped, and the 2023 record sale was $2.006M.

explanation: The stamp is known as the Inverted Jenny after the Curtiss Jenny aircraft, printed flying belly-up because the sheet was fed through the second colour pass the wrong way round.

question: Postage stamps from every country in the world carry the issuing country's name, with a single exception. Which country's stamps are allowed to leave the name off entirely?
topic: Post, stamps and communication before the internet

extra.why_interesting: Players assume every stamp names its country, since that is how postal clerks worldwide sort mail. The one exception is explained by a 'first mover' privilege: the country that invented the stamp never needed to label it, and still doesn't.

explanation: Britain invented the adhesive postage stamp with the Penny Black in 1840, when no other country had stamps to be confused with, and the Universal Postal Union still honours that head start. Instead of a name, the monarch's silhouette identifies British stamps to the rest of the world.
